notes.front: Name two further advantages of fuel injection over a carburettor, besides icing and economy?
notes.back: Improved acceleration, from the positive action of injection; and better fuel distribution, reducing overheating of individual cylinders.
notes.explanation: Uneven distribution often causes the mixture variation that overheats single cylinders.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Fuel-Injection Systems”, p. 2-21
notes.evidence: Acceleration is also improved because of the positive action of the injection system. In addition, fuel injection improves fuel distribution. This reduces the overheating of individual cylinders often caused by variation in mixture due to uneven distribution.

notes.front: An owner’s carburetted engine shows individual cylinders overheating because of uneven mixture distribution. Which change does the handbook say reduces this?
notes.back: B: Converting to fuel injection
notes.choices:
A) Fitting a larger main metering jet
B) Converting to fuel injection
C) Adding a float chamber vent
D) Leaning the mixture further
notes.choicesExplained: A: that richens every cylinder; it does not even out distribution. C: the vent does not affect distribution between cylinders. D: leaning makes the leanest cylinders hotter, not more even.
notes.explanation: Fuel injection improves distribution, which reduces the overheating caused by uneven mixture.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Fuel-Injection Systems”, p. 2-21
notes.evidence: In addition, fuel injection improves fuel distribution. This reduces the overheating of individual cylinders often caused by variation in mixture due to uneven distribution.

notes.front: What are the three sections of the Bendix fuel injector?
notes.back: An airflow section, a regulator section and a fuel metering section.
notes.explanation: Some injectors also carry an automatic mixture control unit.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Fuel Injector”, p. 2-21
notes.evidence: The fuel injector assembly consists of: 1. An airflow section, 2. A regulator section, and 3. A fuel metering section. Some fuel injectors are equipped with an automatic mixture control unit.

notes.front: Why does the Bendix injector have a constant-head idle spring?
notes.back: At low power the venturi pressure difference is too small for consistent fuel regulation.
notes.explanation: The spring provides a constant fuel differential pressure, giving adequate flow in the idle range.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Regulator Section”, p. 2-22
notes.evidence: Under low power settings, the difference in pressure created by the venturi is insufficient to accomplish consistent regulation of the fuel. A constant-head idle spring is

notes.front: In a Bendix injection system the throttle is opened and airflow through the engine increases. What does the air diaphragm do?
notes.back: B: It moves to open the ball valve, as venturi throat pressure falls on one side
notes.choices:
A) It moves to close the ball valve, cutting fuel
B) It moves to open the ball valve, as venturi throat pressure falls on one side
C) It opens the idle cutoff
D) It stays still, because the flow divider sets fuel flow
notes.choicesExplained: A: more airflow lowers throat pressure, which opens the ball valve. D: the flow divider distributes fuel; the injector meters it. C: idle cutoff is selected with the mixture control.
notes.explanation: The pressure difference across the diaphragm is proportional to airflow, so more air means more fuel.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Airflow Section”, p. 2-21
notes.evidence: When airflow through the engine increases, the pressure on the left of the diaphragm is lowered due to the drop in pressure at the venturi throat. [Figure 2-31] As a result, the diaphragm moves to the left, opening the ball valve.

notes.front: In the Bendix system, how does fuel division change between idle and higher flows?
notes.back: At idle the flow divider divides the fuel; above idle, nozzle-line pressure opens it fully and the nozzles govern distribution.
notes.explanation: The divider valve opens only as far as needed to pass the metered fuel.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Flow Divider”, p. 2-23
notes.evidence: the fuel for the individual cylinders is divided at idle by the flow divider. As fuel flow through the regulator is increased above idle requirements, fuel pressure builds up in the nozzle lines. This pressure fully opens the flow divider valve, and fuel distribution to the engine becomes a function of the discharge nozzles.

notes.front: A Bendix-injected engine has a pressure gauge, calibrated in pounds per hour, connected to the flow divider. What is it sensing?
notes.back: A: The pressure applied to the discharge nozzles, which works as a fuel flow reading
notes.choices:
A) The pressure applied to the discharge nozzles, which works as a fuel flow reading
B) Fuel pump inlet pressure
C) Manifold pressure
D) Fuel quantity in the tanks
notes.choicesExplained: B: the gauge is connected to the flow divider, not the pump inlet. C: manifold pressure is an air pressure measured in the induction system. D: it senses pressure in the injection system, not tank contents.
notes.explanation: Nozzle pressure is in direct proportion to fuel flow, so the gauge indicates power output and fuel consumption.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Flow Divider”, p. 2-24
notes.evidence: A fuel pressure gauge, calibrated in pounds per hour fuel flow, can be used as a fuel flow meter with the Bendix RSA injection system. This gauge is connected to the flow divider and senses the pressure being applied to the discharge nozzle.

notes.front: Replacing one injection nozzle on a Continental-injected engine, a mechanic picks up a nozzle stamped with a different range letter from the others. What does the handbook indicate?
notes.back: C: Use a nozzle of the same range letter, because all nozzles for one engine are of the same range
notes.choices:
A) Any letter will do, as the letter is only a part number
B) Fit it, then adjust idle mixture to compensate
C) Use a nozzle of the same range letter, because all nozzles for one engine are of the same range
D) Fit it only on the cylinder nearest the manifold valve
notes.choicesExplained: A: the letter identifies the calibration range. B: the handbook’s rule is that all nozzles for one engine share a range. D: no position-based mixing of ranges is given.
notes.explanation: Nozzles are calibrated in ranges, and a set for one engine must match.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Fuel Discharge Nozzle”, p. 2-27
notes.evidence: Nozzles are calibrated in several ranges, and all nozzles furnished for one engine are of the same range and are identified by a letter stamped on the hex of the nozzle body.

notes.front: Why does the Continental fuel-injection pump need a recirculation path?
notes.back: The pump has more capacity than the engine needs.
notes.explanation: A calibrated orifice and relief valve in the path also keep delivery pressure in proportion to engine speed.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Fuel-Injection Pump”, p. 2-25
notes.evidence: Since the pump provides greater capacity than is required by the engine, a recirculation path is required. By arranging a calibrated orifice and relief valve in this path, the pump delivery pressure is also maintained in proportion to engine speed.

notes.front: In a Continental-injected aircraft the engine-driven pump fails. According to the handbook, what can still provide fuel pressure?
notes.back: B: The auxiliary (boost) pump, whose pressure can bypass the engine-driven pump through a check valve
notes.choices:
A) Nothing; the engine stops immediately
B) The auxiliary (boost) pump, whose pressure can bypass the engine-driven pump through a check valve
C) The fuel manifold valve
D) Ram air in the air throttle
notes.choicesExplained: A: the check valve arrangement lets the auxiliary pump supply pressure. C: the manifold valve divides fuel; it does not pump. D: the air throttle controls airflow; it does not pressurise fuel.
notes.explanation: The same check valve lets boost pressure bypass the engine-driven pump for starting.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Fuel-Injection Pump”, p. 2-25
notes.evidence: A check valve is provided so that boost pump pressure to the system can bypass the engine-driven pump for starting. This feature also suppresses vapor formation under high ambient temperatures of the fuel and permits use of the auxiliary pump as a source of fuel pressure in the event of enginedriven pump failure.

notes.front: In the Continental fuel control assembly, how is fuel flow kept in proportion to airflow?
notes.back: The metering valve is connected to the air throttle.
notes.explanation: Moving the throttle therefore moves air and fuel control together.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Fuel Control Assembly”, p. 2-26
notes.evidence: By connecting the metering valve to the air throttle, the fuel flow is properly proportioned to airflow for the correct airfuel ratio.

notes.front: Before removing a carburettor, which valve must be closed?
notes.back: The fuel shutoff (or selector) valve.
notes.explanation: Then the throttle and mixture linkages are disconnected and the throttle valve lockwired closed.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Carburetor Removal”, p. 2-27
notes.evidence: Before removing a carburetor, make sure the fuel shutoff (or selector) valve is closed. Disconnect the throttle and mixture control linkages, and lockwire the throttle valve in the closed position.

notes.front: Which two checks does the handbook require on a carburettor just before installing it?
notes.back: Proper lockwiring, and removal of all shipping plugs from its openings.
notes.explanation: Both are easy to miss once the unit is bolted on.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Installation of Carburetor”, p. 2-29
notes.evidence: Check the carburetor for proper lockwiring before installation on an engine. Be sure that all shipping plugs have been removed from the carburetor openings.

notes.front: A mechanic installs an overhauled carburettor that uses diaphragms, fills it with fuel, and wants to run the engine an hour later. What does the handbook require?
notes.back: D: Let it stand full of fuel for at least 8 hours first
notes.choices:
A) Run it at once, as diaphragms need no preparation
B) Let it stand full of fuel for 1 hour
C) Let it stand empty and dry for 8 hours
D) Let it stand full of fuel for at least 8 hours first
notes.choicesExplained: A: the diaphragms must be soaked before use. B: the minimum is 8 hours, not 1. C: it must stand filled with fuel, with inlet and vent plugged.
notes.explanation: Soaking makes the diaphragms as pliable as when the unit was originally calibrated.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Installation of Carburetor”, p. 2-29
notes.evidence: Turn off the fuel flow, plug the fuel inlet and vapor vent outlet, and then allow the carburetor, filled with fuel, to stand for a minimum of 8 hours. This is necessary in order to soak the diaphragms and render them pliable to the same degree as when the unit was originally calibrated.

notes.front: How should carburettor throttle linkage springback be adjusted?
notes.back: So springback on the flight deck throttle quadrant is equal at both full-open and full-closed.
notes.explanation: Equal springback shows the carburettor reaches both stops before the quadrant does.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Rigging Carburetor Controls”, p. 2-29
notes.evidence: In addition, check and adjust the throttle control linkages so that springback on the throttle quadrant in the aircraft is equal in both the full-open and full-closed positions.

notes.front: Rigging an unmarked manual mixture control, a mechanic finds springback at the rich end of the quadrant but none at the lean end. What should the adjustment achieve?
notes.back: D: An equal amount of springback at both the rich and lean ends
notes.choices:
A) Springback at the lean end only
B) Springback at the rich end only
C) No springback at either end
D) An equal amount of springback at both the rich and lean ends
notes.choicesExplained: B: the handbook asks for equal springback at both ends. C: springback shows the unit reaches its stops before the quadrant. A: both ends need it, in equal amounts.
notes.explanation: Equal springback at both ends shows the carburettor control moves through its full range.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Rigging Carburetor Controls”, p. 2-29
notes.evidence: When installing carburetors or fuel metering equipment incorporating manual-type mixture controls that do not have marked positions, adjust the mixture control mechanism to provide an equal amount of springback at both the rich and lean ends of the control quadrant in the flight deck

notes.front: Name two effects of excessively rich or lean idle mixtures?
notes.back: Spark plug fouling from carbon deposits; and fast taxi speeds with excessive brake wear from high idle speeds.
notes.explanation: Both come from incomplete combustion and the need to taxi at high idle.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Adjusting Idle Mixtures”, p. 2-29
notes.evidence: Excessively rich or lean idle mixtures result in incomplete combustion within the engine cylinder, with resultant formation of carbon deposits on the spark plugs and subsequent spark plug fouling. In addition, excessively rich or lean idle mixtures make it necessary to taxi at high idle speeds with resultant fast taxi speeds and excessive brake wear.

notes.front: Checking the idle mixture on a conventional carburettor, what rpm rise does the handbook give before speed drops?
notes.back: A rise of 10 to 50 rpm, depending on the installation.
notes.explanation: The mixture is leaned slowly toward idle cutoff, and the rise comes just before the engine ceases to fire.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Adjusting Idle Mixtures”, p. 2-30
notes.evidence: With most installations, the idle mixture should be adjusted to provide an rpm rise prior to decreasing as the engine ceases to fire. This rpm increase varies from 10 to 50 rpm, depending on the installation.

notes.front: Checking idle mixture on a Continental-injected engine, the mechanic slowly moves the mixture toward idle cutoff and the idle speed drops at once with no gain. What does this show?
notes.back: C: The idle mixture is set too lean
notes.choices:
A) The idle mixture is set too rich
B) The idle mixture is correct
C) The idle mixture is set too lean
D) The idle speed stop is set too high
notes.choicesExplained: A: the handbook reads a drop with no gain as too lean, not too rich. B: a correct setting gives a slight, momentary gain first. D: the check is of mixture, shown by the rpm gain or its absence.
notes.explanation: A correct setting gives a slight and momentary gain in idle speed as the mixture moves toward idle cutoff.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Adjusting Idle Mixtures”, p. 2-30
notes.evidence: Adjust to obtain a slight and momentary gain in idle speed as the mixture control is slowly moved toward idle cut off. If the idle mixture is set too lean, the idle speed drops with no gain in speed.

notes.front: A mechanic has just finished setting a carburettor’s idle mixture. What is the next step in the handbook’s sequence?
notes.back: B: Reset the idle stop to the idle rpm given in the aircraft maintenance manual
notes.choices:
A) Readjust the main metering jet
B) Reset the idle stop to the idle rpm given in the aircraft maintenance manual
C) Set the idle stop before checking the mixture again
D) Release the aircraft without further checks
notes.choicesExplained: A: the main jet is not part of idle adjustment. C: idle speed is set after the mixture, not before. D: idle speed must still be set and the engine checked.
notes.explanation: Idle speed is adjusted after the idle mixture, with the engine thoroughly warmed.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Idle Speed Adjustment”, p. 2-30
notes.evidence: After adjusting the idle mixture, reset the idle stop to the idle rpm specified in the aircraft maintenance manual.

notes.front: What does inspection of a fuel system installation basically consist of?
notes.back: An examination for conformity to design requirements, plus functional tests to prove correct operation.
notes.explanation: Systems vary so much that the manufacturer’s instructions must be followed for details.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Fuel System Inspection & Maintenance”, p. 2-31
notes.evidence: The inspection of a fuel system installation consists basically of an examination of the system for conformity to design requirements together with functional tests to prove correct operation.

notes.front: A blister on a fuel hose is pricked with a pin and only air comes out. What should the mechanic do next?
notes.back: C: Pressure-test the hose at 1½ times working pressure; with no fluid leakage it is serviceable
notes.choices:
A) Reject the hose at once
B) Return it to service without testing
C) Pressure-test the hose at 1½ times working pressure; with no fluid leakage it is serviceable
D) Seal the pinhole with sealant and refit
notes.choicesExplained: A: rejection is for a blister that releases fluid. B: a pressure test at 1½ times working pressure comes first. D: no such repair is given; the hose is tested instead.
notes.explanation: Fuel, oil or hydraulic fluid from the pinhole means rejection; air alone calls for the test.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Lines & Fittings”, p. 2-32
notes.evidence: If only air emerges, then test the hose pressure at 11⁄2 times the working pressure. If no fluid leakage occurs, the hose can be regarded as serviceable.

notes.front: What three conditions are checked when inspecting booster pumps?
notes.back: Proper operation; leaks and condition of fuel and electrical connections; and wear of motor brushes.
notes.explanation: Drain lines should also be free of traps, bends or restrictions.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Pumps”, p. 2-32
notes.evidence: During an inspection of booster pumps, check for the following conditions: 1. Proper operation; 2. Leaks and condition of fuel and electrical connections; and 3. Wear of motor brushes.

notes.front: How often is water and sediment drained from the main line strainer?
notes.back: At each preflight inspection.
notes.explanation: The screen itself is removed and cleaned at the periods in the aeroplane maintenance manual.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Main Line Strainers”, p. 2-32
notes.evidence: Drain water and sediment from the main line strainer at each preflight inspection. Remove and clean the screen at the periods specified in the airplane maintenance manual.

notes.front: Cleaning a main line strainer, a mechanic finds particles of rubber in the sediment. What does the handbook say these often warn of?
notes.back: A: Hose deterioration
notes.choices:
A) Hose deterioration
B) A worn float needle valve
C) Water contamination of the fuel
D) A normal build-up needing no action
notes.choicesExplained: B: rubber particles are linked to hoses in the handbook. C: water is drained separately; rubber points elsewhere. D: the handbook calls them an early warning.
notes.explanation: Sediment is examined because it can point to where the contamination came from.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Main Line Strainers”, p. 2-32
notes.evidence: Examine the sediment removed from the housing. Particles of rubber are often early warnings of hose deterioration.

notes.front: When inspecting a fuel pressure gauge, what is checked on the instrument itself?
notes.back: The pointer for zero tolerance and excessive oscillation, and the cover glass for looseness and proper range markings.
notes.explanation: Lines and connections are also checked for leaks and the vent for obstruction.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Fuel Pressure Gauge”, p. 2-32
notes.evidence: Check the pointer for zero tolerance and excessive oscillation. Check the cover glass for looseness and for proper range markings. Check the lines and connections for leaks.

notes.front: Inspecting a fuel selector, a mechanic finds the handle points to a tank position but worn linkage leaves the valve part-way between positions. What is the concern?
notes.back: C: Restricted fuel flow that can seriously reduce engine power
notes.choices:
A) None, as long as the handle placard is legible
B) Only a wrong fuel quantity reading
C) Restricted fuel flow that can seriously reduce engine power
D) Vapour lock in the tank vents
notes.choicesExplained: A: placards do not help if the valve itself is mispositioned. B: the valve position affects fuel flow to the engine. D: the issue is restriction of fuel flow at the valve.
notes.explanation: Worn mechanical linkage is one cause of inaccurate selector valve positioning.
notes.source: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B (Change 1), ch. 8, par. 8-34d, p. 8-26
notes.evidence: Inaccurate positioning of fuel selector valves can also be caused by worn mechanical linkage between the selector handle and the valve unit. An improper fuel valve position setting can seriously reduce engine power by restricting the available fuel flow.

notes.front: How is internal leakage of a cross-feed, firewall shutoff or tank selector valve checked?
notes.back: Set the valve to off, drain the fuel strainer bowl, and watch whether fuel keeps flowing into it.
notes.explanation: Fuel reaching the bowl with the valve off can only be leaking past the valve.
notes.source: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B (Change 1), ch. 8, par. 8-34a, p. 8-25
notes.evidence: Internal leakage can be checked by placing the appropriate valve in the “off” position, draining the fuel strainer bowl, and observing if fuel continues to flow into it.

notes.front: Fuel stains are found around a firewall shutoff valve mounted under the cabin floor. How does Advisory Circular 43.13-1B treat this?
notes.back: A: As a possible severe fire hazard; the cause of the stains must be corrected
notes.choices:
A) As a possible severe fire hazard; the cause of the stains must be corrected
B) As acceptable if the valve still shuts off
C) As cosmetic, needing only cleaning
D) As a matter for the next annual inspection only
notes.choicesExplained: C: the circular says to correct the cause of any fuel stains. B: external leakage is the hazard, whatever the valve’s function. D: no deferral is given; the cause is to be corrected.
notes.explanation: External leakage is especially dangerous in a confined area such as under the cabin floor.
notes.source: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B (Change 1), ch. 8, par. 8-34b, p. 8-26
notes.evidence: External leakage from these units can result in a severe fire hazard, especially if the unit is located under the cabin floor or within a similarly confined area. Correct the cause of any fuel stains associated with fuel leakage.

notes.front: Where fuel lines cannot be separated from electrical wiring, how must they be placed?
notes.back: Below the wiring, clamped securely to the airframe structure.
notes.explanation: Wiring must never be supported by the fuel line.
notes.source: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B (Change 1), ch. 8, par. 8-31b, p. 8-23
notes.evidence: Where physical separation of the fuel lines from electrical wiring or conduit is impracticable, locate the fuel line below the wiring and clamp it securely to the airframe structure. In no case should wiring be supported by the fuel line.

notes.front: Why must a fuel line between two rigidly mounted fittings include at least one bend?
notes.back: To absorb strain caused by vibration and temperature changes.
notes.explanation: A straight tube between rigid fittings has no way to flex.
notes.source: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B (Change 1), ch. 8, par. 8-31c, p. 8-23
notes.evidence: Never install a straight length of tubing between two rigidly mounted fittings. Always incorporate at least one bend between such fittings to absorb strain caused by vibration and temperature changes.

notes.front: For metallic fuel lines of 3/8 to 1/2 inch outside diameter, supports go approximately every {{c1::16}} inches.
notes.explanation: Larger tubes are supported at longer spacings, up to 40 inches for 1 1/2 to 2 inch tube.
notes.source: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B (Change 1), ch. 8, par. 8-31f, p. 8-23

notes.front: Replacing a fuel line, a mechanic finds two fittings that look interchangeable but come from different series. What does Advisory Circular 43.13-1B warn?
notes.back: D: They may differ in thread pitch or design, preventing proper mating and letting the joint leak or fail
notes.choices:
A) Any fittings that screw together are compatible
B) Mixing is fine if the joint is torqued higher
C) Only the tube material matters, not the fittings
D) They may differ in thread pitch or design, preventing proper mating and letting the joint leak or fail
notes.choicesExplained: A: appearance and threading together do not prove compatibility. B: extra torque does not correct a mismatch. C: all fittings must be compatible with their mating parts.
notes.explanation: All fittings are to be compatible with their mating parts.
notes.source: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B (Change 1), ch. 8, par. 8-31a, p. 8-23
notes.evidence: Although various types of fittings appear to be interchangeable, in many cases they have different thread pitch or minor design differences which prevent proper mating and may cause the joint to leak or fail.

notes.front: According to whose instructions are boost, emergency, auxiliary and engine-driven fuel pumps inspected, repaired and overhauled?
notes.back: The appropriate manufacturer’s instructions.
notes.explanation: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B gives no pump procedures of its own.
notes.source: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B (Change 1), ch. 8, par. 8-35, p. 8-26
notes.evidence: Inspect, repair, and overhaul boost pumps, emergency pumps, auxiliary pumps, and engine-driven pumps in accordance with the appropriate manufacturer’s instructions.

notes.front: How must fuel strainer bowls be installed?
notes.back: According to the direction of the fuel flow.
notes.explanation: A bowl fitted backwards would not strain the fuel as designed.
notes.source: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B (Change 1), ch. 8, par. 8-36, p. 8-26
notes.evidence: Examine fuel strainer bowls to see that they are properly installed according to the direction of the fuel flow.

notes.front: A fuel filter element is found contaminated. Besides replacing it with the recommended type, what does Advisory Circular 43.13-1B require?
notes.back: A: Determine and correct the source of the contaminants
notes.choices:
A) Determine and correct the source of the contaminants
B) Nothing more; replacement solves it
C) Clean and refit the throwaway element
D) Fit a coarser filter so it clogs less
notes.choicesExplained: B: the source of contamination must be found and corrected. C: throwaway elements are replaced with the recommended type. D: the recommended type must be used.
notes.explanation: Replacing the element alone would leave the cause in place.
notes.source: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B (Change 1), ch. 8, par. 8-36, p. 8-26
notes.evidence: Check each strainer and filter element for contamination. Determine and correct the source of any contaminants found. Replace throwaway filter elements with the recommended type.

notes.front: During fuel system work, what must be done with open fuel lines?
notes.back: They must be capped.
notes.explanation: This is one of the circular’s listed fire and explosion precautions.
notes.source: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B (Change 1), ch. 8, par. 8-38c, p. 8-26
notes.evidence: c. Open fuel lines must be capped.

notes.front: When may a metal fuel tank be welded or soldered?
notes.back: Only after it has been adequately purged of fuel fumes.
notes.explanation: Keeping a tank or cell filled with carbon dioxide prevents explosion of the fumes.
notes.source: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B (Change 1), ch. 8, par. 8-38e, p. 8-26
notes.evidence: e. Metal fuel tanks must not be welded or soldered unless they have been adequately purged of fuel fumes. Keeping a tank or cell filled with CO2 will prevent explosion of fuel fumes.

notes.front: Before starting a fuel system repair on an aircraft in the hangar, which of these is one of the precautions listed in Advisory Circular 43.13-1B?
notes.back: C: Properly ground the aircraft
notes.choices:
A) Remove the propeller
B) Drain every tank completely
C) Properly ground the aircraft
D) Disconnect all flight controls
notes.choicesExplained: A: this is not among the circular’s listed fuel precautions. B: draining is not among the listed precautions. D: this has nothing to do with fuel fire safety.
notes.explanation: Grounding is listed first because fuel is flammable and the danger of fire or explosion always exists.
notes.source: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B (Change 1), ch. 8, par. 8-38a, p. 8-26
notes.evidence: a. Aircraft being serviced or having the fuel system repaired must be properly grounded.

notes.front: Which two handling risks do the Airman Certification Standards list for engine fuel and fuel metering systems?
notes.back: Handling fuel metering system components, and handling engine fuel control units, that may contain fuel.
notes.explanation: The standards also list fuel control adjustment and maintenance considerations among the task’s risks.
notes.source: Aviation Mechanic General, Airframe, and Powerplant Airman Certification Standards (FAA-S-ACS-1), Powerplant Area III, Task I, Risk Management
notes.evidence: AM.III.I.R3 Handling of fuel metering system components that may contain fuel. AM.III.I.R4 Considerations during fuel system maintenance. AM.III.I.R5 Handling of engine fuel control units that may contain fuel.

notes.front: What does Advisory Circular 43.13-1B require of fuel indicator systems?
notes.back: Inspection, servicing and adjustment per the manufacturer’s instructions, with required placards and markings complete and legible.
notes.explanation: Illegible markings would make a working indicator misleading.
notes.source: Advisory Circular 43.13-1B (Change 1), ch. 8, par. 8-37, p. 8-26
notes.evidence: Inspect, service, and adjust the fuel indicator systems according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Determine that the required placards and instrument markings are complete and legible.

notes.front: With anti-detonation injection, what provides the cooling that excess fuel used to give?
notes.back: Vaporisation of the water-alcohol mixture.
notes.explanation: That lets the mixture be leaned to the setting that produces maximum power.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Water Injection Systems for Reciprocating Engines”, p. 2-33
notes.evidence: With the injection of the antidetonant fluid, the mixture can be leaned out to that which produces maximum power, and the vaporization of the water-alcohol mixture then provides the cooling formerly supplied by the excess fuel.

notes.front: On which engines was water injection mostly used?
notes.back: Large radial engines; it has very limited use in modern aircraft engines.
notes.explanation: It let those engines make more takeoff power than without it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Water Injection Systems for Reciprocating Engines”, p. 2-33
notes.evidence: These systems have very limited use in modern aircraft engines. Water injection was used mostly on large radial engines. The water injection system enabled more power to be obtained from the engine at takeoff than is possible without water injection.

notes.front: Why does a turbine fuel control need a water injection speed reset servo?
notes.back: Without it, the fuel control would decrease rpm, so no extra thrust would result during water injection.
notes.explanation: The servo resets the speed adjustment to a higher value while water flows.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Water Injection System”, p. 2-40
notes.evidence: A water injection speed reset servo resets the speed adjustment to a higher value during water injection. Without this adjustment, the fuel control would decrease rpm so that no additional thrust would be realized during water injection.

notes.front: What is rich blowout in a turbine engine?
notes.back: Loss of combustion when there is too little oxygen to support it and excess fuel cools the mixture below combustion temperature.
notes.explanation: It results when fuel becomes excessive in relation to mass airflow.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Turbine Engine Fuel System—General Requirements”, p. 2-33
notes.evidence: Rich blowout occurs when the amount of oxygen in the air supply is insufficient to support combustion and when the mixture is cooled below the combustion temperature by the excess fuel.

notes.front: During a rapid acceleration, a turbine’s fuel flow is increased faster than the engine can accept. What might result, according to the handbook?
notes.back: A: An over-rich mixture, with the possibility of rich blowout or compressor stall
notes.choices:
A) An over-rich mixture, with the possibility of rich blowout or compressor stall
B) Vapour lock in the fuel manifold
C) Lean flameout
D) A cooler turbine and faster spool-up
notes.choicesExplained: C: lean flameout comes from too little fuel, not too much. B: the risk named is over-richness in the combustor. D: the handbook names rich blowout or compressor stall, not any cooling or faster spool-up.
notes.explanation: Acceleration needs extra energy, but fuel added too quickly overshoots.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Turbine Engine Fuel System—General Requirements”, p. 2-33
notes.evidence: However, if the fuel flow increases too rapidly, an over rich mixture can be produced, with the possibility of a rich blowout or compressor stall.

notes.front: What are the three basic groups of gas turbine engine fuel controls?
notes.back: Hydromechanical, hydromechanical/electronic, and FADEC.
notes.explanation: Most turbine fuel controls are quickly moving to the FADEC type.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Turbine Fuel Controls”, p. 2-33
notes.evidence: Gas turbine engine fuel controls can be divided into three basic groups: 1. Hydromechanical, 2. Hydromechanical/electronic, and 3. Full Authority Digital Engine (or Electronics) Control (FADEC).

notes.front: A turbine fuel control uses electronic inputs and outputs with servo motors setting fuel flow, but can also run purely hydromechanically. Which basic group is it?
notes.back: C: Hydromechanical/electronic
notes.choices:
A) Pure hydromechanical
B) True FADEC
C) Hydromechanical/electronic
D) A pressure carburettor
notes.choicesExplained: A: a pure hydromechanical control has no electronic interface at all. B: a true FADEC has no hydromechanical backup. D: that is a reciprocating-engine metering device.
notes.explanation: The hybrid type can function solely as a hydromechanical control.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Turbine Fuel Controls”, p. 2-33
notes.evidence: The hydromechanical/electronic fuel control is a hybrid of the two types of fuel control but can function solely as a hydromechanical control. In the dual mode, inputs and outputs are electronic, and fuel flow is set by servo motors.

notes.front: Hydromechanical versus electronic fuel controls: which meters fuel more accurately, and why?
notes.back: Electronic controls, which can receive more inputs with greater accuracy.
notes.explanation: The handbook adds that hydromechanical operating procedures are very complicated.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Hydromechanical Fuel Control”, p. 2-34
notes.evidence: Actual operating procedures for a hydromechanical fuel control is very complicated and still the fuel metering is not as accurate as with an electronic type of interface or control. Electronic controls can receive more inputs with greater accuracy than hydromechanical controls.

notes.front: A turbine fuel control is driven by the gas generator gear train to sense engine speed and has no electronic interface in computing or metering. Which type is it?
notes.back: A: A pure hydromechanical fuel control
notes.choices:
A) A pure hydromechanical fuel control
B) A FADEC fuel control
C) A hydromechanical/electronic control in automatic mode
D) An electronic engine control
notes.choicesExplained: B: FADEC depends entirely on electronic sensors and outputs. C: in automatic mode the electronic unit meters the fuel. D: the EEC is a computer, the opposite of this.
notes.explanation: Having no electronic interface is what defines the pure hydromechanical control.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Hydromechanical Fuel Control”, p. 2-34
notes.evidence: A pure hydromechanical fuel control has no electronic interface assisting in computing or metering the fuel flow. It also is generally driven by the gas generator gear train of the engine to sense engine speed.

notes.front: In the handbook’s hydromechanical/electronic example, what happens if the electronic fuel control unit fails?
notes.back: The fuel control assembly runs in manual mode, allowing operation at reduced power under hydromechanical control only.
notes.explanation: The pilot can also choose manual mode deliberately.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Hydromechanical/Electronic Fuel Control”, p. 2-34
notes.evidence: In the event of electrical or EFCU failure, or at the option of the pilot, the fuel control assembly functions in manual mode to allow engine operation at reduced power under control of the hydromechanical portion of the controller only.

notes.front: In the example system, how do primary and secondary nozzles flow during and after a start?
notes.back: During start all flow goes through the primaries; as demand rises the secondaries open, and in steady running both flow.
notes.explanation: The flow divider valve does the switching.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Hydromechanical/Electronic Fuel Control”, p. 2-36
notes.evidence: During an engine start, the flow divider directs all flow through the primary nozzles. After start, as the engine fuel demand increases, the flow divider valve opens to allow the secondary nozzles to function. During all steady-state engine operation, both primary and secondary nozzles are flowing fuel.

notes.front: In the handbook’s auxiliary power unit FADEC control, what filter does fuel meet first, and what if it clogs?
notes.back: A 10-micron filter; if it is contaminated, the pressure drop opens a bypass valve and unfiltered fuel reaches the unit.
notes.explanation: Bypassing keeps fuel flowing at the cost of filtration.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “FADEC for an Auxiliary Power Unit”, p. 2-36
notes.evidence: Fuel entering the fuel control unit first passes through a 10-micron filter. If the filter becomes contaminated, the resulting pressure drop opens the filter bypass valve and unfiltered fuel then is supplied to the APU.

notes.front: A technician is asked to trim a FADEC-controlled turbofan’s fuel control mechanically. What does the handbook say?
notes.back: D: Most electronic fuel controls need no trimming; changes are made by software or by changing the EEC
notes.choices:
A) Trim it exactly like a hydromechanical control
B) Adjust the programming plug wiring
C) Adjust the fuel metering valve by hand
D) Most electronic fuel controls need no trimming; changes are made by software or by changing the EEC
notes.choicesExplained: A: most electronic controls do not require trimming or mechanical adjustments. C: the metering valve only follows EEC commands. B: the plug selects software; it is not a trim adjustment.
notes.explanation: In a FADEC system the computing is done by the EEC, so changes go through it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Fuel Control Maintenance”, p. 2-41
notes.evidence: Most electronic control fuel control systems do not require trimming or mechanical adjustments. Changes to the EEC in the FADEC system is normally accomplished through software changes or changing the EEC.

notes.front: How many channels does the turbofan EEC have, and what can each do?
notes.back: Two; each is an independent computer that can completely control the engine.
notes.explanation: Either channel alone can run the engine if the other is unavailable.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “FADEC Fuel Control Propulsion Engine”, p. 2-38
notes.evidence: The EEC is a two channel computer that controls every aspect of engine operation. Each channel, which is an independent computer, can completely control the operation of the engine.

notes.front: What does the EEC’s cross-talk logic do?
notes.back: Compares data from channels A and B to choose the better channel to drive each torque motor or solenoid bank.
notes.explanation: The primary channel drives all outputs unless the other is better for a given bank.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “FADEC Fuel Control Propulsion Engine”, p. 2-38
notes.evidence: The cross-talk logic compares data from channels A and B and uses the cross-talk logic to find which EEC channel is the best to control the output driver for a torque motor or solenoid bank.

notes.front: An EEC is being removed from a high-bypass turbofan for replacement. What happens to its programming plug?
notes.back: D: It stays with the engine, tethered to the fan case by a lanyard
notes.choices:
A) It goes with the old EEC to the workshop
B) It is discarded and a new one fitted
C) It is fitted to the replacement EEC before removal
D) It stays with the engine, tethered to the fan case by a lanyard
notes.choicesExplained: A: the plug remains with the engine. B: the plug is kept; it selects the engine’s thrust rating software. C: it is simply left attached to the engine.
notes.explanation: The plug selects the software for the engine’s thrust rating, so it belongs to the engine, not the computer.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “FADEC Fuel Control Propulsion Engine”, p. 2-39
notes.evidence: The programming plug selects the proper software in the EEC for the thrust rating of the engine. The plug attaches to the engine fan case with a lanyard. When removing the EEC, the plug remains with the engine.

notes.front: After the fuel metering unit, what path does metered fuel take to the combustor?
notes.back: Through the fuel flow transmitter to the distribution valve, then the fuel supply manifolds and the fuel injectors.
notes.explanation: The injectors spray the metered fuel into the engine for combustion.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Fuel System Operation”, p. 2-40
notes.evidence: Fuel for combustion (metered fuel) goes through the fuel flow transmitter to the distribution valve. [Figure 2-57] The fuel distribution valve supplies metered fuel to the fuel supply manifolds. [Figure 2-58] The fuel injectors get the metered fuel from the fuel supply manifolds and spray the fuel into the engine for combustion.

notes.front: In the FADEC turbofan fuel system, the filter differential pressure switch signals an almost clogged filter, and the element then clogs completely. What happens?
notes.back: C: Unfiltered fuel bypasses the filter element
notes.choices:
A) The engine shuts down at once
B) The EEC switches to a backup hydromechanical control
C) Unfiltered fuel bypasses the filter element
D) Fuel returns to the tank until the filter is changed
notes.choicesExplained: A: the system allows bypass so fuel keeps flowing. B: a true FADEC has no hydromechanical backup. D: the handbook describes bypass around the element.
notes.explanation: The switch warns the EEC first, so the clogging is known before bypass begins.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Fuel System Operation”, p. 2-40
notes.evidence: The fuel filter differential pressure switch supplies a signal to the EEC that indicates an almost clogged filter condition. Unfiltered fuel can then bypass the filter element if the element becomes clogged.

notes.front: Which adjustments may be made to a turbine fuel control in the field?
notes.back: The idle rpm and the maximum speed adjustment, commonly called trimming the engine.
notes.explanation: Both are made in the normal range of operation.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Fuel Control Maintenance”, p. 2-40
notes.evidence: These adjustments are limited to the idle rpm and the maximum speed adjustment, commonly called trimming the engine. Both adjustments are made in the normal range of operation.

notes.front: During engine trimming, what four things is the fuel control checked for?
notes.back: Idle rpm, maximum rpm, acceleration and deceleration.
notes.explanation: The exact procedure varies with the aircraft and engine installation.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Fuel Control Maintenance”, p. 2-40
notes.evidence: During engine trimming, the fuel control is checked for idle rpm, maximum rpm, acceleration, and deceleration. The procedures used to check the fuel control vary depending on the aircraft and engine installation.

notes.front: Why must engine trimming be done under precisely controlled conditions, with the aircraft into wind?
notes.back: To ensure the minimum thrust level on which the aircraft’s performance is based.
notes.explanation: Precise trimming also contributes to better engine life.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Fuel Control Maintenance”, p. 2-41
notes.evidence: Engine trimming should always be carried out under precisely controlled conditions with the aircraft headed into the wind. Precise control is necessary to ensure maintenance of a minimum thrust level upon which the aircraft performance is based.

notes.front: A crew plans to trim a turbine engine this morning in freezing fog, with ice forming on the aircraft. What does the handbook say?
notes.back: D: Do not trim: engines should never be trimmed if icing conditions exist
notes.choices:
A) Trim, but only the idle rpm
B) Trim, but add five minutes to stabilisation
C) Trim with the aircraft tail into wind
D) Do not trim: engines should never be trimmed if icing conditions exist
notes.choicesExplained: B: the rule is never to trim in icing conditions. C: the aircraft should head into wind, and icing rules out trimming anyway. A: no partial trimming in icing conditions is allowed.
notes.explanation: Adjusting a turbine fuel control is one of the task’s named risks; icing is a condition the handbook rules out entirely.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Fuel Control Maintenance”, p. 2-41
notes.evidence: Engines should never be trimmed if icing conditions exist.

notes.front: What type is the main (second) stage of a turbine engine-driven fuel pump, generally?
notes.back: A positive-displacement pump.
notes.explanation: Positive displacement means the gears supply a fixed quantity of fuel for every revolution.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Main Fuel Pumps (Engine Driven)”, p. 2-41
notes.evidence: The second or main stage of the engine-driven fuel pump for turbine engines is generally a positive displacement type of pump. The term “positive displacement” means that the gear supplies a fixed quantity of fuel to the engine for every revolution of the pump gears.

notes.front: Why does a gear-type main fuel pump need a pressure relief valve?
notes.back: Sized for all conditions, it has excess capacity over most of its range, and the surplus must be bypassed to the inlet.
notes.explanation: Its flow rises in a near straight line with speed while engine needs fluctuate.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Main Fuel Pumps (Engine Driven)”, p. 2-41
notes.evidence: Gear-type pumps have approximately straight line flow characteristics, whereas fuel requirements fluctuate with flight or ambient air conditions. Hence, a pump of adequate capacity at all engine operating conditions has excess capacity over most of the range of operation. This is the characteristic that requires the use of a pressure relief valve for bypassing excess fuel back to the inlet.

notes.front: A technician plans to turn a turbine engine’s fuel pump for a long period with no fuel supplied to the pump inlet. What does the handbook warn?
notes.back: C: The pump is lubricated by the fuel passing through it and should never be turned without fuel flow
notes.choices:
A) No concern, because the pump is oil-lubricated
B) It is fine if the relief valve is open
C) The pump is lubricated by the fuel passing through it and should never be turned without fuel flow
D) Only the boost stage can be damaged
notes.choicesExplained: A: the handbook says the fuel itself lubricates the pump. B: the relief valve does not supply lubrication. D: the warning applies to the pump as a whole.
notes.explanation: The same reason is why fuel should be supplied until the pump stops during coast-down at shutdown.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Main Fuel Pumps (Engine Driven)”, p. 2-42
notes.evidence: The fuel pump is also lubricated by the fuel passing through the pump, and it should never be turned without fuel flow supplied to the inlet of the pump. As the engine coasts down at shutdown, the fuel pump should be provided with fuel until it comes to a stop.

notes.front: At what fuel temperature does residual water in turbine fuel tend to freeze, and why does that matter?
notes.back: At 32 °F or below; the ice crystals can be trapped in the filter and block fuel flow to the engine.
notes.explanation: The handbook calls a blocked filter a very serious problem, so the fuel is kept above freezing.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Fuel Heater”, p. 2-42
notes.evidence: When the fuel in the aircraft fuel tanks cools to 32 °F or below, residual water in the fuel tends to freeze, forming ice crystals. When these ice crystals in the fuel become trapped in the filter, they block fuel flow to the engine, which causes a very serious problem.

notes.front: After a cold soak, the fuel filter ice warning comes on. According to the handbook, can the fuel heater help?
notes.back: B: Yes: it can be used to thaw ice on the fuel screen so fuel flows freely again
notes.choices:
A) No: the heater only prevents ice and cannot remove it
B) Yes: it can be used to thaw ice on the fuel screen so fuel flows freely again
C) No: only removing the filter clears the ice
D) Yes, but only by heating the tanks
notes.choicesExplained: A: the handbook says it can also thaw ice on the screen. C: the heater is named as a way to thaw it. D: the heater warms the fuel system, not the tanks.
notes.explanation: Its main function is protection from ice, but thawing a blocked screen is a named second use.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Fuel Heater”, p. 2-42
notes.evidence: The function of a fuel heater is to protect the engine fuel system from ice formation. However, should ice form in the filter, the heater can also be used to thaw ice on the fuel screen to allow fuel to flow freely again.

notes.front: Why does a micron filter need a bypass valve?
notes.back: Its minute openings make it susceptible to clogging.
notes.explanation: The handbook calls the bypass valve a necessary safety factor.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Fuel Filters”, p. 2-42
notes.evidence: The minute openings make this type of filter susceptible to clogging; therefore, a bypass valve is a necessary safety factor.

notes.front: A filter is wanted between the fuel tank and the engine that also absorbs water before it reaches the pumps. Which type fits best?
notes.back: D: A micron filter with a cellulose element
notes.choices:
A) A plain screen mesh filter
B) A 74-micron self-bypassing screen
C) No filter; the boost pump removes water
D) A micron filter with a cellulose element
notes.choicesExplained: A: a plain mesh does not have the micron filter’s thorough action or water absorption. B: that is a last-chance screen before the nozzles. C: the boost pump releases vapour; it does not remove water.
notes.explanation: The handbook singles out the micron filter as especially valuable between tank and engine.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Fuel Filters”, p. 2-42
notes.evidence: Since the micron filter does such a thorough job of removing foreign matter, it is especially valuable between the fuel tank and engine. The cellulose material also absorbs water, preventing it from passing through the pumps.

notes.front: Hot streaking marks are found inside a combustion liner, and at one spot the liner is burned. What nozzle problem does the handbook link to this?
notes.back: B: Fuel not evenly distributed and well centred in the flame area
notes.choices:
A) Nozzles delivering too fine a spray
B) Fuel not evenly distributed and well centred in the flame area
C) Too little fuel pressure at idle only
D) A combustion drain valve stuck open
notes.choicesExplained: A: fine atomisation is the design aim, not a fault. C: the handbook links hot spots to uneven, off-centre distribution. D: drain valves deal with accumulated fuel, not the spray pattern.
notes.explanation: Even, centred fuel prevents hot spots and hot streaking and stops the flame burning through the liner.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Fuel Spray Nozzles & Fuel Manifolds”, p. 2-43
notes.evidence: It is very important that the fuel be evenly distributed and well centered in the flame area within the liners. This is to preclude the formation of any hot spots or hot streaking in the combustion chambers and to prevent the flame burning through the liner.

notes.front: Simplex versus duplex nozzle: what manifolding does each need?
notes.back: Duplex usually needs a dual manifold and a pressurising valve or flow divider; simplex needs only a single manifold.
notes.explanation: The duplex has two fuel flows to keep separate; the simplex has one.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Fuel Spray Nozzles & Fuel Manifolds”, p. 2-43
notes.evidence: The duplex nozzle usually requires a dual manifold and a pressurizing valve or flow divider for dividing primary and secondary (main) fuel flow, but the simplex nozzle requires only a single manifold for proper fuel delivery.

notes.front: Why should the fuel nozzles in one turbine engine be matched?
notes.back: So they flow equal amounts of fuel.
notes.explanation: Even fuel distribution is important to efficient combustion in the burner section.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Fuel Spray Nozzles & Fuel Manifolds”, p. 2-44
notes.evidence: The nozzles used in a specific engine should be matched so that they flow equal amounts of fuel. Even fuel distribution is important to efficient combustion in the burner section.

notes.front: What does each simplex fuel nozzle consist of?
notes.back: A nozzle tip, an insert, and a strainer of fine-mesh screen with a support.
notes.explanation: Its single path means only a single manifold is needed.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Simplex Fuel Nozzle”, p. 2-44
notes.evidence: Each of the simplex nozzles consists of a nozzle tip, an insert, and a strainer made up of fine-mesh screen and a support.

notes.front: An older turbine engine starts and idles with poor atomisation. Its nozzles are the first type used in turbine engines, fed from a single manifold. Which type are they?
notes.back: D: Simplex nozzles
notes.choices:
A) Duplex nozzles
B) Bendix air-bleed injection nozzles
C) Airblast nozzles of the duplex kind
D) Simplex nozzles
notes.choicesExplained: A: the duplex replaced the simplex because it atomised better at starting and idle. C: duplex types need a dual manifold. B: those serve reciprocating engines, one per cylinder.
notes.explanation: The duplex nozzle was brought in because it gave better atomisation at starting and idling speeds.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Simplex Fuel Nozzle”, p. 2-44
notes.evidence: The simplex fuel nozzle was the first nozzle type used in turbine engines and was replaced in most installations with the duplex nozzle, which gave better atomization at starting and idling speeds.

notes.front: During a start only the primary orifices of the duplex nozzles are flowing. What opens the path to the secondary manifold as fuel flow rises?
notes.back: C: The flow divider bellows compressing at a predetermined differential pressure
notes.choices:
A) The combustion drain valve closing
B) The pilot selecting a secondary switch
C) The flow divider bellows compressing at a predetermined differential pressure
D) The EEC programming plug
notes.choicesExplained: A: the drain valve closes on chamber pressure but does not route fuel. B: the change is automatic, driven by pressure. D: the plug selects software for thrust rating.
notes.explanation: Rising flow raises the differential pressure on the bellows until the valve opens.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Flow Divider”, p. 2-45
notes.evidence: When fuel flow increases, the differential pressure on the bellows also increases. At a predetermined pressure, the bellows compresses, allowing the flow divider valve to open. This action starts fuel flow to the secondary manifold, which increases the fuel flow to the engine.

notes.front: Give two advantages of airblast nozzles?
notes.back: Lower working pressures, allowing lighter pumps, and less tendency to carbon up.
notes.explanation: Carbon build-up can disturb the flow pattern, so reducing it matters.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Airblast Nozzles”, p. 2-45
notes.evidence: This nozzle type can operate at lower working pressures than other nozzles which allows for lighter pumps. This airblast nozzle also helps in reducing the tendency of the nozzle to carbon up which can disturb the flow pattern.

notes.front: What does the pressurising valve’s positive cutoff prevent?
notes.back: Fuel dribbling into the manifold and through the nozzles, which limits afterfires and nozzle carbonisation.
notes.explanation: The valve traps fuel forward of the manifold to give this cutoff.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Fuel Pressurizing & Dump Valves”, p. 2-46
notes.evidence: manifold, giving a positive cutoff. This cutoff prevents fuel from dribbling into the manifold and through the fuel nozzles, limiting afterfires and carbonization of the fuel nozzles.

notes.front: What is a drip or dump valve, and how may it be operated?
notes.back: A unit that drains the fuel manifolds; it may work by pressure differential or be solenoid operated.
notes.explanation: It is used in some instances instead of other drain arrangements.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Combustion Drain Valves”, p. 2-46
notes.evidence: In some instances, the fuel manifolds are drained by an individual unit known as a drip or dump valve. This type of valve may operate by pressure differential, or it may be solenoid operated.

notes.front: After shutdown, a turbine engine’s nozzles keep dribbling fuel and afterfires occur. Which unit’s cutoff is most suspect?
notes.back: B: The fuel pressurising valve
notes.choices:
A) The fuel heater
B) The fuel pressurising valve
C) The EEC programming plug
D) The airblast swirl vanes
notes.choicesExplained: A: the heater controls fuel temperature, not cutoff. D: swirl vanes mix air and fuel while running. C: the plug selects software for thrust rating.
notes.explanation: A pressurising valve’s positive cutoff stops fuel dribbling into the manifold and nozzles, limiting afterfires.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Fuel Pressurizing & Dump Valves”, p. 2-46
notes.evidence: manifold, giving a positive cutoff. This cutoff prevents fuel from dribbling into the manifold and through the fuel nozzles, limiting afterfires and carbonization of the fuel nozzles.

notes.front: When is a combustion drain valve open, and when closed?
notes.back: A spring holds it open; chamber pressure closes it during operation, and it drains when pressure falls near atmospheric.
notes.explanation: Being closed while running stops combustion gases escaping through it.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Combustion Drain Valves”, p. 2-46
notes.evidence: the drain valve allows the fuel to be drained whenever pressure within the manifold or the burner(s) has been reduced to near atmospheric pressure. A small spring holds the valve off its seat until pressure in the combustion chamber during operation overcomes the spring and closes the valve. The valve is closed during engine operation.

notes.front: A turbine engine’s combustion drain valve is stuck closed. What does the handbook say is likely?
notes.back: B: A hot start on the next start, or an afterfire after shutdown
notes.choices:
A) Nothing, because the valve is closed during running anyway
B) A hot start on the next start, or an afterfire after shutdown
C) A lean flameout at cruise
D) Vapour lock in the fuel manifold
notes.choicesExplained: A: it must open after shutdown to drain accumulated fuel. C: the drain valve deals with fuel left after shutdown or a false start. D: the risk named is accumulated fuel, not vapour.
notes.explanation: The valve must be in good working condition to drain accumulated fuel after each shutdown.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Combustion Drain Valves”, p. 2-46
notes.evidence: It is imperative that this valve be in good working condition to drain accumulated fuel after each shutdown. Otherwise, a hot start during the next starting attempt or an afterfire after shutdown is likely to occur.

notes.front: Can-type versus annular combustion chambers: how does accumulated fuel reach the drain valve?
notes.back: Can type: by gravity through flame or interconnector tubes to the lower chambers. Annular: through the air holes in the liner.
notes.explanation: In both, the combustion chamber drain valve then removes fuel left after shutdown or a false start.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 2, “Combustion Drain Valves”, p. 2-46
notes.evidence: If the combustion chambers are the can type, fuel drains by gravity down through the flame tubes or interconnector tubes until it gathers in the lower chambers, which are fitted with drain lines to the drain valve. If the combustion chamber is of the basket or annular type, the fuel merely drains through the air holes in the liner

notes.front: How can many turbine fuel nozzles be checked after cleaning?
notes.back: By flowing fluid through the nozzle under pressure and closely checking the flow pattern.
notes.explanation: Each part is also inspected for nicks and burrs before the flow check.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Fuel Nozzle & Support Assemblies”, p. 10-50
notes.evidence: Inspect each component part of the fuel nozzle assembly for nicks and burrs. Many fuel nozzles can be checked by flowing fluid through the nozzle under pressure and closely checking the flow pattern coming for the nozzle.

notes.front: A technician wants to remove stubborn carbon from a turbine fuel nozzle with a wire brush. What does the handbook advise?
notes.back: D: Do not: soften deposits with approved cleaning fluid and a soft bristle brush, since scraping or wire brushing can impair spray characteristics
notes.choices:
A) Wire brush it, then flow check it
B) Leave the carbon, since it does not affect the spray
C) Scrape it with a hard tool instead
D) Do not: soften deposits with approved cleaning fluid and a soft bristle brush, since scraping or wire brushing can impair spray characteristics
notes.choicesExplained: A: the handbook says no attempt should be made to clean nozzles with a wire brush. C: scraping with a hard implement is ruled out for the same reason. B: all carbon deposits are to be cleaned from the nozzles.
notes.explanation: The spray characteristics of the nozzle may become impaired by hard cleaning.
notes.source: Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook–Powerplant (FAA-H-8083-32B), ch. 10, “Fuel Nozzle & Support Assemblies”, p. 10-50
notes.evidence: Because the spray characteristics of the nozzle may become impaired, no attempt should be made to clean the nozzles by scraping with a hard implement or by rubbing with a wire brush.
